messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Crowding: Crowded places, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Vignette:
Imran, a 76-year-old South Asian man who had spent most of his adult life working as an electrician, described the robbery as the moment his ordinary routines split into a before and after. It happened years ago, late in the evening, when he was coming home with tools from a job and was approached by strangers who mugged him before he could react. He did not dwell on every detail in a dramatic way; instead, he spoke with a steady, clipped tone that made it clear how much the event still sat in his body. What stayed with him most was not a single image but the sense of being overtaken by people he had not expected to be dangerous. Since then, he has become much more alert to strangers approaching him in ordinary situations. Even now, if someone he does not know comes toward him on the street, or turns toward him too quickly, he feels a sharp tightening of attention and instinctively braces himself. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and he finds himself watching hands, shoulders, and body position before he can focus on what is being said.

In the months after the mugging, Imran noticed that nighttime felt different from daytime in a way he could not dismiss. He had once been accustomed to moving comfortably between his work, errands, and home, but after the robbery he began to feel less safe after dark. He said that during the day he could manage, though he remained watchful, but at night the uneasiness became harder to shake. He started checking doors more than once and feeling unsettled when he had to step outside after dusk. This was especially difficult because his work as an electrician sometimes involved finishing a job later than planned, and the shift into evening could leave him tense long before he was actually in any danger. He was aware that the street, the parking lot, or the front path to his home could all feel more threatening once the light dropped, and he found himself arranging his movements to avoid unnecessary exposure at night whenever possible.

His sense of alarm also followed him into crowded places. Imran used to handle busy environments as part of ordinary life, but after the mugging he began to notice how quickly a crowd could make him feel cornered and exposed. In shops, waiting areas, and public spaces, he became more careful about where people were standing and how close they were moving. Crowds were no longer just inconvenient; they felt unpredictable, with too many bodies, too many directions, too little control. He said he tried to keep to the edges of rooms and avoid being trapped in the middle of a packed space. This had practical consequences in daily life. Outings that had once been routine now took more planning, and he sometimes chose not to go somewhere if he expected it to be busy. His wife noticed that he preferred quieter hours and less crowded routes, and he acknowledged that he had become the kind of man who always seemed to be looking for an exit.

Certain sensory reminders brought him back to the robbery in a more immediate way. He reported that the smell of alcohol was especially unsettling. If he passed someone who had been drinking, or caught the odor in a public place, he felt an abrupt wave of unease that seemed to place him back near the men who attacked him. He did not describe a detailed flashback, but rather a sharp internal jolt, as if the atmosphere itself had changed. That smell made the world feel less predictable, and he became eager to move away from it quickly. Because alcohol could be encountered in ordinary public settings, this added another layer to the way he scanned his surroundings and chose where to stand or how long to remain somewhere.

Sleep brought its own difficulties. Imran reported waking from nightmares with a residue that lingered into the morning. On those nights, he would wake disoriented and tense, and the feeling from the dream did not simply disappear when he opened his eyes. He might sit up, listen to the house, and take a while to settle himself before he could return to sleep. He spoke about these mornings as if they were tainted by whatever had happened in the dream, leaving him already on edge before the day had even begun. Over time, these nights added to a sense that his body was not fully resting, and that he had to start each day from a place of alertness rather than ease.

By the time he came for help, Imran had lived with these changes for long enough that they had become part of family life and daily planning. His wife had adapted to his preference for quieter places and earlier returns home, but he could see that it affected how they moved through the world together. He sought help now because the combination of waking from nightmares, feeling unsafe at night, becoming tense around strangers and sudden movements, and avoiding crowded places had started to feel like too much to manage alone. He did not say he wanted to forget the mugging entirely; what he hoped for was simpler and more practical. He wanted to feel safer moving through ordinary life again, especially after dark, and to stop living as though every stranger, crowd, or smell of alcohol might mean trouble was about to start.
